faq.question: Who makes Studio Monjo notebooks?
faq.answer: I’m Jordan Monnet, a French maker in Seoul. I fold, sew and check each notebook by hand in my studio.

faq.question: What paper do Robey notebooks use?
faq.answer: Robey notebooks have blank 105gsm pages chosen for handwriting, including fountain pens. Removable lined and grid guide sheets slip beneath the page when you want them.

faq.question: Where can I buy a notebook?
faq.answer: For delivery in South Korea, order through the Studio Monjo Naver shop. For an international order, message Studio Monjo on Instagram with your notebook choice and delivery country. I’ll confirm availability, shipping and payment details.

faq.question: Can I order notebooks for my company?
faq.answer: Yes. Company editions start at 20 copies. Choose a white cover with your logo or an original Robey illustration, with your message inside. Share your quantity, timing and idea through the company enquiry form.

about.title: Our story
about.description: Meet Jordan Monnet, the French maker behind Studio Monjo in Seoul, and discover why he makes notebooks by hand for writing, drawing and personal stories.
about.eyebrow: Jordan Monnet · The maker behind Studio Monjo
about.heading:
Why I make
notebooks.
about.intro: I’m a French maker in Seoul. I fold, sew and check every notebook myself. But what interests me most is what happens after it leaves my hands.
about.portraitAlt: Jordan smiling at his market table, surrounded by the notebooks he makes
about.portraitCaption: Out of the studio, meeting the people who will fill these pages.
origin: My grandmother learned to write with a dip pen. I grew up with fountain pens. Later, I spent many years working in artificial intelligence. The tools changed, but the physical act of writing stayed with me: a pen, ink, paper, and the pause before a line.
Working among words that can be generated so quickly made me appreciate something else: taking the time to write by hand and allowing a thought to wander. Studio Monjo began with that feeling.
A notebook makes room for that time. You can turn an idea over, cross something out, draw beside it, or leave a page unfinished. It holds the way you think, as well as the words you finally choose.
making: Folding the sheets, drawing the thread through the spine, checking a finished notebook: these are small, repeated actions, but they make the object personal. Every notebook carries some of my time and attention.

I leave the pages blank. There are lined and grid guides if you need them, but no prescribed way to fill the book. I want the care I put into making it to become an invitation for someone else to use it.
about.pull:
A notebook carries my time.
Then it begins to carry yours.
robey: Robey is a small robot meeting the human world for the first time. Through his eyes, I draw moments we can become too used to seeing: falling petals, a library, a walk beneath the trees.

I want to look again at what makes us human, and at the things that make our world beautiful and surprising. Each illustrated notebook holds the beginning of that story. Its blank pages leave room for yours.
about.marketTitle: The story that stayed with me.
market: At a market, a child became absorbed in Robey’s story. They wanted to draw inside the notebook and invent his next adventure, and worked hard to persuade their mother.

When the notebook was finally theirs, they asked me to write a short message on the first page. I loved the thought that a story I had begun could continue in someone else’s imagination. I still hope that notebook is filling up with their own wonderful stories.

That is why meeting people at markets matters to me. I hear what they see in a cover, what they feel about Robey, and what they want to put on the pages. These encounters stay with me when I return to the studio.
